MEMB. 3. SUBSECT. 1.

Air rectified. With a digression of the Air.

As a long-winged Hawk when he is first whistled off the fist, mounts aloft, and for his pleasure fetcheth many a circuit in the Air, still soaring higher and higher, till he be come to his full pitch, and in the end when the game is sprung, comes down amain, and stoops upon a sudden: so will I, having now come at last into these ample fields of Air, wherein I may freely expatiate and exercise myself for my recreation, awhile rove, wander round about the world, mount aloft to those ethereal orbs and celestial spheres, and so descend to my former elements again. In which progress, I will first see whether that relation of the Friar of aa note Nich. de Lynna cited by Mercator in his Map.Oxford be true, concerning those Northern parts under the Pole (if I meet ob­i­terTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.in passinggon the waydjby the way [in passing] with the wandering Jew, Elias Artifex, or Lucian’s Icaromenippus, they shall be my guides), whether there be such 4 Euripes, and a great rock of Loadstones, which may cause the needle in the Compass still to bend that way, and what should be the true cause of the variation of the compass, bb note Mons Sloto. Lessius's point is that his sphere, which holds 800,000 millions, is more than big enough. Jason Pratensis, in his book de morbis capitis§, and chapter of Melancholy, hath these words out of Galen, °° note Veniant ad me audituri quo esculento, quo item poculento uti debeant, et praeter alimentum ipsum, potumque ventos ipsos docebo, item aeris ambientis temperiem, insuper regiones quas eligere, quas vitare ex usu sit. dmAuthor trans. “Let them come to me to know what meat and drink they shall use, and besides that, I will teach them what temper of ambient Air they shall make choice of, what wind, what countries they shall choose, and what avoid” Let them come to me to know what meat and drink they shall use, and besides that, I will teach them what temper of ambient Air they shall make choice of, what wind, what countries they shall choose, and what avoid. Out of which lines of his, thus much we may gather, that to this cure of melancholy, amongst other things the rectification of Air is necessarily required. This is performed, either in reforming Natural or Artificial Air. Natural, is that which is in our election to choose or avoid: and ’tis either general, to Countries, Provinces; particular, to Cities, Towns, Villages, or private houses. What harm those extremities of heat or cold do in this malady, I have formerly showed: the medium must needs be good, where the Air is temperate, serene, quiet, free from bogs, fens, mists, all manner of putrefaction, contagious and filthy noisome smells. The Clime changeth not so much customs, manners, wits (as Aristotle Polit. lib. 6 cap. 4§, Vegetius, Plato, Bodin method. hist. cap. 5§ have proved at large), as constitutions of their bodies, and temperature itself. In all particular Provinces we see it confirmed by experience, as the Air is, so are the inhabitants, dull, heavy, witty, subtle, neat, cleanly, clownish, sick, and sound. The best soil commonly yields the worst air, a dry sandy plat is fittest to build upon, and such as is rather hilly than plain, full of Downs, a Cotswold country, as being most commodious for hawking, hunting, wood, waters, and all manner of pleasures. Perigord in France is barren, yet by reason of the excellency of the air, and such pleasures that it affords, much inhabited by the Nobility; as Nuremberg in Germany, Toledo in Spain. Our countryman Tusser will tell us so much, that the fielden is for profit, the woodland for pleasure and health, the one commonly a deep clay, therefore noisome in Winter, and subject to bad highways: the other a dry sand. Provision may be had elsewhere, and our Towns are generally bigger in the woodland than the fielden, more frequent and populous, and Gentlemen more delight to dwell in such places. Sutton Coldfield in Warwickshire (where I was once a Grammar Scholar) may be a sufficient witness, which stands, as Camden notes, loco in­grato & ste­riliTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.in an unpleasant and barren spotgin a bad and barren situation,djin an unkindly and barren spot Burton cites: William Camden, Britannia (unverified)ingratus, used of land, means land that gives a poor return for the work put into it. [in an unpleasant and barren spot], but in an excellent air, and full of all manner of pleasures. ee note The seat of George Purefoy, Esq.Wadley in Berkshire is situate in a vale, though not so fertile a soil as some vales afford, yet a most commodious site, wholesome, in a delicious air, a rich and pleasant seat. He that respects not this in choosing of his seat, or building his house, is ⁂mente cap­tusTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Burton translates: “mad”Burton’s own rendering out of his mind , mad, ll cites Lib. 1 cap. 2.Cato saith, and his dwelling next to Hell itself, according to Columella: he commends in conclusion, the middle of an hill, upon a descent. Baptista Porta Villae, lib. 1 cap. 22§, censures Varro, Cato, Columella, and those ancient Rustics, approving many things, disallowing some, and will by all means have the front of an house stand to the South, which how it may be good in Italy and hotter climes, I know not, in our Northern countries I am sure it is best: Stephanus a Frenchman, praedio rustic. lib. 1 cap. 4§, subscribes to this, approving especially the descent of an hill South or South-East, with trees to the North, so that it be well watered; a condition in all sites which must not be omitted, as Herberstein inculcates, lib. 1§. If it be so the natural site may not be altered of our City, Town, Village, yet by artificial means it may be helped. In hot countries therefore they make the streets of their Cities very narrow, all over Spain, Africk, Italy, Greece, and many Cities of France, in Languedoc especially, and Provence, those Southern parts: Montpellier, the habitation and University of Physicians, is so built, with high houses, narrow streets to divert the Sun’s scalding rays, which Tacitus commends, lib. 15 Annal.§, as most agreeing to their health, °° note Quoniam angustiae itinerum et altitudo tectorum, non perinde Solis calorem admittit. dmAuthor trans. “because the height of buildings, and narrowness of streets, keep away the Sunbeams” because the height of buildings, and narrowness of streets, keep away the Sunbeams. Some Cities use Galleries, or arched Cloisters towards the street, as Damascus, Bologna, Padua, Berne in Switzerland, Westchester with us, as well to avoid tempests, as the Sun’s scorching heat. They build on high hills in hot countries, for more air; or to the seaside, as Baiae, Naples, &c. In our Northern coasts we are opposite, we commend straight, broad, open, fair streets, as most befitting and agreeing to our clime. We build in bottoms for warmth: and that site of Mytilene in the Island of Lesbos, in the Aegean Sea, which Vitruvius so much discommends, magnificently built with fair houses, ⁂sed im­pru­den­ter po­si­tamTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Burton translates: “unadvisedly sited”Burton’s own rendering but unwisely sited , unadvisedly sited, because it lay along to the South, and when the South wind blew, the people were all sick, would make an excellent site in our Northern climes.

Of that artificial site of houses I have sufficiently discoursed: if the seat of the dwelling may not be altered, yet there is much in choice of such a chamber or room, in opportune opening and shutting of windows, excluding foreign air and winds, and walking abroad at convenient times. nn cites Consil. 21 lib. 2.Johannes Crato von Krafftheim, consilium 21, book 2.Crato a German commends East and South site (disallowing cold air and Northern winds in this case, rainy weather and misty days), free from putrefaction, fens, bogs, and muckhills. If the air be such, open no windows, come not abroad. The best site for chamber windows in my judgement are North, East, South, and which is the worst, West. Levinus Lemnius lib. 3 cap. 3 de occult. nat. mir.§ attributes so much to air, and rectifying of wind and windows, that he holds it alone sufficient to make a man sick or well; to alter body and mind. pp note Di­scu­tit Sol hor­ro­rem crassi spi­ri­tus, men­tem ex­hi­la­rat, non enim tam cor­pora, quam & animi mu­ta­tio­nem inde su­beunt, pro coeli & ven­to­rum ra­tione, & sani ali­ter af­fecti sint coelo nu­bilo, ali­ter se­renoTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Completing Burton’s rendering:The sun dispels the chill of a heavy spirit and gladdens the mind, for it is not bodies so much as minds that thereby experience change, by reason of the sky and the winds, and the healthy are affected in one way by a cloudy sky, in another by a clear onegThe sun dispels the gloom of a thick air and cheers the mind; for not only our bodies but our minds too undergo change from it, according to the state of the sky and the winds, and even healthy people are affected one way in cloudy weather and another in clear. Great heed is therefore to be taken at what times we walk, how we place our windows, lights, and houses, how we let in or exclude this ambient air. The Egyptians, to avoid immoderate heat, make their windows on the top of the house like chimneys, with two tunnels to draw a through air. Although our ordinary air be good by nature or art, yet it is not amiss, as I have said, still to alter it; no better Physic for a melancholy man than change of air and variety of places, to travel abroad and see fashions. vv note Lib. 1, cap. de morb. Paulus Aemilius, that renowned Roman Captain, after he had conquered Perseus, the last king of Macedonia, and now made an end of his tedious wars, though he had long been absent from Rome, and much there desired, about the beginning of Autumn (as aa cites Lib. 45.Livy, book 45.Livy describes it) made a pleasant peregrination all over Greece, accompanied with his son Scipio, and Athenaeus the brother of King Eumenes, leaving the charge of his army with Sulpicius Gallus. By Thessaly he went to Delphos, thence to Megaris, Aulis, Athens, Argos, Lacedaemon, Megalopolis, &c. [more for showing-off than for the benefit of the commonwealth] (as bb cites Keckermann praefat. polit.Bartholomaeus Keckermann, Systema disciplinae politicae, preface .one well observes), to crack, gaze, see fine sights and fashions, spend time, rather than for his own or public good (as it is to many gallants that travel out their best days, together with their means, manners, honesty, religion), yet it availeth howsoever. For peregrination charms our senses with such unspeakable and sweet variety, cc cites Fynes Moryson cap. 3 part. 1.Fynes Moryson, chapter 3, part 1.that some count him unhappy that never travelled, a kind of prisoner, and pity his case, that from his cradle to his old age beholds the same still; still, still the same, the same. Insomuch that °° note Mutatio de loco in locum, Itinera, et voiagia longa et indeterminata, et hospitare in diversis diversoriis. dmAuthor trans. “enjoin travel, and such variety of objects to a melancholy man, and to lie in diverse Inns” Moving from place to place; long journeys with no fixed end. A good prospect alone will ease melancholy, as Gomesius contends, lib. 2 cap. 7 de Sale§. The citizens of dd note In Catalonia in Spain.Barcino, saith he, otherwise penned in, Melancholy, and stirring little abroad, are much delighted with that pleasant prospect their city hath into the sea, which like that of old Athens besides Aegina, Salamina, and many pleasant Islands, had all the variety of delicious objects: so are those Neapolitans, and inhabitants of Genoa, to see the ships, boats, and passengers go by, out of their windows, their whole cities being sited on the side of an hill, like Pera by Constantinople, so that each house almost, hath a free prospect to the sea, as some part of London to the Thames: or to have a free prospect all over the city at once, as at Granada in Spain, and Fez in Africk, the river running betwixt two declining hills, the steepness causeth each house almost, as well to oversee, as to be overseen of the rest. Every country is full of such ee note Lau­da­tur­que domus lon­gos quae pro­spi­cit agrosTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Source: Horace, Epistulae, 1.10 text matched by rule in perseus-latin (text-match-v2)A house which overlooks wide fields is commendedgAnd the house is praised that looks out over far-stretching fields. In Egypt the square top of the great Pyramid 300 yards in height, and so the Sultan’s Palace in Grand Cairo, the country being plain, hath a marvellous fair prospect as well over Nilus, as that great city, five Italian miles long, and two broad, by the riverside: from mount Sion in Jerusalem the holy land is of all sides to be seen: such high places are infinite: with us those of the best note are Glastonbury Tower, Belvoir Castle, Radway Grange, gg note Lately resigned for some special reasons.Walesby in Lincolnshire, where I lately received a real kindness, by the munificence of the right honourable my noble Lady and patroness, the Lady Frances Countess Dowager of Exeter: and two amongst the rest, which I may not omit for vicinity’s sake, Oldbury in the confines of Warwickshire, where I have often looked about me with great delight, at the foot of which hill hh note At Lindley in Leicestershire, the possession and dwelling-place of Ralph Burton Esquire, my late deceased father.I was born: and Hanbury in Staffordshire, contiguous to which is Fauld a pleasant Village, and an ancient patrimony belonging to our family, now in the possession of mine elder brother William Burton Esquire. ii note In Icon animorum.Barclay the Scot commends that of Greenwich tower for one of the best prospects in Europe, to see London on the one side, the Thames, ships, and pleasant meadows on the other. There be those that say as much and more of St. Mark’s steeple in Venice. Yet these are at too great a distance; some are especially affected with such objects as be near, to see passengers go by in some great Roadway, or boats in a river, ⁂in su­b­jec­tum forum de­spi­cereTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Burton translates: “to oversee a Fair, a Marketplace”Burton’s own rendering to look down on the market-place below , to oversee a Fair, a Marketplace, or out of a pleasant window into some thoroughfare street to behold a continual concourse, a promiscuous rout, coming and going, or a multitude of spectators at a Theatre, a Masque or some such-like show. But I rove: the sum is this, that variety of actions, objects, air, places, are excellent good in this infirmity and all others, good for man, good for beast. jj note Ae­gro­tan­tes oves in alium locum tran­spor­tan­dae sunt, ut alium aerem & aquam par­ti­ci­pan­tes, coa­le­scant & cor­ro­bo­ren­turTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Sickly sheep are to be transported to another place, so that by partaking of different air and water they can become stronger and be invigoratedgSick sheep should be moved to another place, so that by taking in a different air and water they may recover and grow strong. Burton cites: Constantine (Geoponica), after Leontius, lib. 18 cap. 13 (unverified)coalescant here means 'recover, gather strength'. [Sickly sheep are to be transported to another place, so that by partaking of different air and water they can become stronger and be invigorated].Sickly sheep are to be transported to another place, so that by partaking of different air and water they can become stronger and be invigorated gConstantine the Emperor lib. 18 cap. 13 ex Leontio§, holds it an only cure for rotten sheep, and any manner of sick cattle. Laelius à fonte Eugubinus that great Doctor, at the latter end of many of his consultations (as commonly he doth set down what success his Physic had), in melancholy most especially approves of this above all other remedies whatsoever, as appears consult. 69, consult. 229, &c.§, °° note Alia utilia, sed ex mutatione aeris potissimum curatus. dmAuthor trans. “Many other things helped, but change of air was that which wrought the cure, and did most good” Many other things helped, but change of air was that which wrought the cure, and did most good.

"The exceeding riches of his grace." Eph. ii. 7. -- Ex*ceed"ing*ness, n w gloss sited Having a site; situated w note long-winged Hawk Falcon.note sprung Made by the hunting hound to fly up into the air, where it is to be seized by the hawk.gloss amain At full speed, or full force.gloss stoops Swoops.note the wandering Jew, Elias Artifex, or Lucian’s Icaromenippus Three mythical or fictional itinerants: the ‘Wandering Jew’, said to be cursed to roam the earth until the Second Coming; Menippus, who in Lucian’s Icaromenippus, or The Sky-Man takes a trip up to the heavens to visit the citadel of Zeus; on ‘Elias Artifex’, see above, .about such 4 Euripes, and a great rock of Loadstones ‘Euripes’ here refers generically to straits or sea channels – cf. above, . Burton is alluding to the report, made by the Carmelite friar and astronomer Nicholas of Lynne (fl. 1386–1411), that at the North Pole there were four channels of water flowing into a massive central whirlpool, and that at the pole itself there was a black mountain of magnetic rock, thirty-three miles in circumference, which was the source of the earth’s magnetic field. In note ‘g’, ‘Mons Sloto’, which was described as the highest mountain in the world by the Italian philosopher Francesco Patrizi in his Nova de universis philosophia (1591), has not been identified.note the variation of the compass Magnetic declination, whereby the angle on the horizontal plane between magnetic north and true north varies depending on one’s geographical location.about some other star in the bear That is, a star in Ursa Minor, as specified by the Italian philosopher and astrologer Marsilio Ficino (1433–99).about magnetical meridian A distinct locality that is magnetic – in fact a magnetic island, according to the Sicilian astronomer Francesco Maurolico (1494–1575).note by and by 12, and then 22 That is, the magnetic declination varies from 7° to 12° and then 22°, depending on one’s position.about Rasceburg Raseborg (or Raasepori).about Bartison the Hollander The Dutch navigator and cartographer Willem Barentsz (c. 1550–97).note fretum Davis, or Nova Zembla Two places that are representative, respectively, of the Northwest and Northeast Passage to Asia (the latter was sought by Barentsz): the Davis Strait, in the Labrador Sea between Greenland and Canada; and Novaya Zemlya, an archipelago in the Arctic Ocean that separates the Barents Sea from the Kara Sea.about Fox A list of explorers and navigators who were engaged in the search for a Northwest Passage from what is now Hudson Bay. Henry Hudson (d. 1611) sailed through what would later be called the Hudson Strait into the bay in 1610. ‘Hubbard’s Hope’, now Hubbard Point on the bay’s west coast near Churchill, was named after Josias Hubart (or ‘Hubbard’), the pilot of one of the ships of Thomas Button (c. 1575–1634). The island named by Luke Fox (1586–1635) as ‘Sir Thomas Roe’s Welcome’ – after the diplomat Sir Thomas Roe, who had sponsored the expedition in which it was discovered – was north of the point in latitude 62° 42′ N that had been named by Button ‘Ne ultra’ (‘No farther’), and redescribed by Fox as ‘Ut ultra’ (‘That much farther’) in his North-West Fox (1635); it is now Roes Welcome Sound at the northwest end of Hudson Bay.gloss Cards Plan, or chart.note that California is … an Island The misconception of the Baja California Peninsula as a large island, separated from the mainland by a strait (now the Gulf of California), originated in Spanish reports and maps from the sixteenth century, and persisted into the eighteenth century.about Neap tides These occur shortly after the first or third quarters of the moon, when the high-water level is at the lowest point, and there is the smallest difference between high- and low-water levels (in contrast to ‘spring tides’ after a new or full moon, when the difference is greatest).note the straits of Anian … by the Promontory of Tabin The Strait of Anian was a mythical passage thought to form the final stretch of the Northwest Passage, sometimes said to run between what is now far-eastern Russia and Alaska, either near the Bering Strait or farther south. On Tabin, see above, .about Quinsay Or ‘Kinsai’, modern-day Hangzhou.about Cambalu A corruption of ‘Khanbaliq’, which had been the capital of the Mongol Empire since the reign of Kublai Khan (1260–94), and now Beijing.note whether … China and Cataia be all one By the seventeenth century it had become widely accepted in Europe that China and Cathay (‘Cataia’ or ‘Catai’) were the same place.note the great Cham of Tartary Khan, the title given to the rulers of the Tartars and Mongols.about Xuntain … Paquin ‘Xuntain’ was more usually spelled ‘Xuntien’, another name for what is now Hangzhou; it was sometimes confused with Beijing (Peking), which was also called ‘Paquin’ as well as ‘Cambalu’.about Presbyter John Or ‘Prester John’, a mythical Christian king and patriarch thought, in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, to have ruled a Christian ‘Church of the East’. His kingdom was sometimes located in Asia (particularly India) or Africa (particularly Ethiopia).about Guinea The island of New Guinea.about that hungry Spaniard’s … Terra Australis Incognita In 1603, the Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós (1563–1615) had been commissioned by Philip III of Spain to discover ‘the Unknown Southern Continent’ (the mythical terra australis), which had been the subject of speculation since antiquity, and was often seen in the early modern period as a second ‘new world’ to be explored and colonized.about Magellanica The regions of Patagonia visited by the Portuguese explorer Magellan (Fernão de Magalhães, 1480–1521) in 1520.about Mercurius Britannicus … Lucinia Joseph Hall’s satirical and fictional Mundus alter et idem (1605) contained lands called ‘Locania’ and ‘Larcinia’, either of which may be intended here.about Schouten and Le Maire The Dutch navigators Willem Schouten (fl. 1590–1619) and Jacob Le Maire (1585–1616) sailed around Cape Horn in 1616.gloss discovery Exploration.note that great Bird Rucke Usually spelled ‘roc’ (or ‘rukh’), a legendary giant bird of prey that originated in Indian mythology and was popularized in Arabic folklore; Marco Polo claimed that it had come to Madagascar from regions farther south.about Gryphs Griffins, which according to a Scythian myth related by Herodotus, guarded gold against the thievery of the ‘one-eyed’ people of the Arimaspians.gloss fountains Here, founts or sources.note flowing Flooding (the regular overflowing of the Nile had been observed since antiquity).about Senega The Senegal River in northwest Africa, forming the border between Mauritania and Senegal.note those Etesian winds Northwesterly winds in the Mediterranean, blowing for about forty days in the summer (or, more generally, any winds that blow annually from a particular region).about Mount Libanus Mount Lebanon in northern Syria.about Maragnan, Orenoque … Zona Torrida The Marañón River in Peru, the principal source of the Amazon; the Orinoco River, running through Venezuela and into Colombia; and the ‘Torrid Zone’ – see above, .about Cauchinchina Cochinchina, a region in southern Vietnam that includes Saigon and centres on the Mekong Delta.about pacifico The Pacific Ocean (after its Spanish name, ‘Mar del Zur’).about Moabar The Coromandel Coast in southeastern India.about Mount … Pelion … Ossa Mounts Pelion and Ossa in Greece.about Meteors Any atmospheric or meteorological phenomena.source 1,250 paces … Dicaearchus Pliny the Elder (2.65) reports that the ancient Greek philosopher Dicaearchus of Messana calculated the height of Mount Pelion as 1,250 paces, which is just over 6,000 feet (or 1,850 metres).about 78 miles … Caucasus On Italian miles – presumably the measurement used by the Italian scholar Jacopo Mazzoni (1548–98) – see above, .note 32 stadiums A ‘stadium’ is a Greek and Roman measure of length, usually one-eighth of a Roman mile, and regarded by later writers as equivalent to a ‘furlong’ (220 yards).note Manoa, or Eldorado in that golden Empire Manõa, the mythical ‘Lost City of Gold’ renowned for its riches, was often identified in Renaissance sources as El Dorado, the realm of the ‘Golden King’. Confusion reigned about its location, but it was often said to be in what is now Colombia or northern Brazil.about gigantical Patagons in Chica In note ‘f’, ‘Patagons’ were a mythical race of giants thought by many explorers to have inhabited the region known sometimes as ‘Chica’, and later as Patagonia.about Ybouyapab in the Northern Brazil The Serra de Ibiapaba, a mountain range on the boundary between the Brazilian states of Ceará and Piauí.note that of Pariacaca … in Peru Mount Pariacaca in the Peruvian Andes.about The pike of Tenerife Mount Teide, or the Pico del Teide, a volcano on Tenerife in the Canary Islands.about underground A reference to Lake Cerknica, a seasonal lake in the region of Inner Carniola in modern-day Slovenia. It is connected to a series of underground caverns, and its size varies throughout the year, with a maximum depth of about twenty feet but sometimes disappearing completely. On a map of Carniola produced by the Austrian cartographer Wolfgang Lazius (1514–65), first published in 1561, a note printed close to the town of Vrhnika (Oberlaibach in German) claimed that the Argonauts travelled from there towards the Adriatic by passing through an underground cave that had been hollowed out of a mountain.note in Muscovia A cave at the Swedish city of Viborg (in present-day Russia), called ‘the Bang’ (in Swedish, ‘Smällen’), perhaps on account of an episode from 1495, famous in local folklore, when the city’s governor created an explosion inside the cave, harnessing the magnifying effect of its echo to scare off Russian invaders.about Gilbert’s Cave in Lapland On the island of Visingsö, on Lake Vättern in Sweden: it is named after the apprentice of the sorcerer Kettil Runske, who, according to a legend recorded by Olaus Magnus in his Historia de gentibus septentrionalibus (1555), imprisoned Gilbert in the cave as a punishment.gloss exonerates Discharges.about Jaxares, Oxus The Syr Darya (formerly River Jaxartes) and Amu Darya (formerly River Oxus), originating from what are now the border regions, respectively, of Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, and of Tajikistan and Afghanistan, both used to run into the Caspian Sea.note the mouth of Oby The mouth of the Ob River is in northern Russia, where it flows into the Arctic Ocean.note the Mexican lake Lake Texcoco, then in the Valley of Mexico.note the Titicacan in Peru … Terapeia Lake Titicaca, on the border of Peru and Bolivia, and Lake Tarapaya in Bolivia.gloss exhalation Evaporation.about Mare mortuum The Dead Sea.about Thrasumene Lake Trasimeno, near Perugia in central Italy.about Padus The River Po.about Rhodanus The River Rhône.source Danubius According to Strabo (Geography 7.1.5), the sources (‘fountains’) of the Danube were actually discovered by the emperor Tiberius, a day’s march north of Lake Constance, in 15 BCE.about Trajan’s bridge In 105 CE, Trajan did build a bridge across the Danube, near what is now Drobeta-Turnu Severin in Romania; also known as the Bridge of Apollodorus, after its architect, it is thought to be the longest built by the Romans.about Grotta de Sibylla The Grotto of the (Cumaean) Sibyl, part of a network of transport tunnels built in the late first century BCE, was previously thought to run through the acropolis at Cumae, though archaeologists now think it was sited elsewhere in Cumae or at Baiae (a Roman resort on the Bay of Naples).source Lucullus’ Fishponds According to Plutarch (Lucullus 39), the Roman general Lucullus – see above, – had a vast set of artificial waterworks, which included streams for breeding fish, built at his famously luxurious villa at the resort of Baiae.note the Temple of Nidrose Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim, Norway, which was built over period of 230 years between 1070 and 1300, and was historically an important pilgrimage site.about Alpine mice Alpine marmots, which hibernate for up to nine months in a year.gloss convicts Proves.about Spanish Kites Red kites – the Italian historian and travel writer Pietro Martire d’Anghiera specifies the bird called ‘Milvus Regalis’ by the Spanish, in his De legatione Babylonica (1533).about Isthmi, Euripi, Chersonesi Isthmuses, sea channels and peninsulas; on ‘Euripi’, see above, ; ‘Chersonesi’ derives from the Greek term for a peninsula (χερσόνησος).gloss baths Hot or mineral springs.note places Here, perhaps, farms or farmsteads (but several alternative meanings are possible, including battlefields, buildings, houses, estates and public or residential squares).about Remora The echeneis, or sucking-fish, which attaches itself to ships (and other objects) and thereby was said to delay them (mora means delay in Latin); their apparently magical power was of interest in the Renaissance.about Zoophytes Plants thought to have some qualities of animals.about Herberstein his Tartar lamb The Austrian diplomat and travel writer Sigismund Freiherr von Herberstein (1486–1566) identifies this plant as ‘barometz’. This was a fake specimen, of obscure origins, often said to be a plant–animal hybrid, and made from the creeping rootstock and frond-stalks of the woolly fern (Cibotium barometz). It was more commonly called the ‘Scythian Lamb’, but its putative origins in Tartary were of continued interest in the seventeenth century.note goose-bearing tree in the Orcades The barnacle goose, or ‘tree goose’, which visits British coasts (including the Orkney Islands) only in winter, was once thought to be produced by a tree growing by the sea-shore, either from its fruit, or from a shell on the tree, or from a kind of mushroom generated by the rotting of its timber in the water.about Hispaniola An island in the Greater Antilles of the Caribbean.note those spherical stones … others relate While the stones in the shapes of animals were presumably fossils, the nature and purpose of the other objects reportedly excavated remains unclear. The carved stone spheres (or man-made ‘petrospheres’), remarked upon by Spanish explorers, were presumably similar to the Diquís spheres in Costa Rica. In this passage ‘Mansfield’ is Mansfeld Land, in southwestern Saxony-Anhalt in Germany, a region once ruled by the counts of Mansfeld; ‘Nokow and Pallukie’ are the villages of Nochowo and Pałuki in central Poland, just south of Poznań and north of Warsaw respectively.note business The extraordinary characteristics of the inhabitants of the mythical land of ‘Lukomorye’ (or ‘Lukomorje’), located on some maps in Muscovy or Siberia, were described by several travel writers in this period.gloss Seamen Mermen.gloss just Full, complete.note that terrestrial Paradise The Garden of Eden.source Ophir … Peruana … Aurea Chersonesus Ophir is the famously wealthy port from which, according to the Bible (1 Kings 10:22), King Solomon regularly received a cargo of gold and other precious materials. Renaissance commentators speculated whether this lay in Africa, the Americas or Asia. The passage here refers to Peru and the Malay Peninsula (the ‘Golden Chersonese’ in the works of classical geography) as possibilities.about Patrick’s Purgatory A pilgrimage site containing a cave said to be the entrance to purgatory, located on Station Island in County Donegal, Ireland.about Trophonius’ den The ancient oracle of the god Trophonius, at Lebadea in western Boeotia, was consulted by descending underground, and was said to have involved a terrifying confrontation with the god himself rather than a medium. As Erasmus recorded in his Adagia, the notorious experience of having ‘descended into Trophonius’ cave’ and emerging sombrely dejected later became a proverbial description of someone who has become ‘extremely sorrowful and gloomy’.note Hecla in Iceland, Etna in Sicily See above, 1.2.1.2, p. 196.note his meteors That is, his Meteorologica.gloss Equinoctial Equator.gloss reciprocally Alternately.note pure element That is, wholly comprising one of the four natural elements (earth, air, fire and water).gloss Chaos Environment, or space.note that Ambrosian College in Milan The Biblioteca Ambrosiana, which was named after the patron saint of Milan, opened in 1609 as a centre of Catholic Counter-Reformation scholarship.gloss schoolmen Scholastic theologian (or philosopher).about Lipari One of the volcanic Aeolian Islands, the largest in a chain running between Vesuvius and Etna. Sometimes the name refers to the entire group, which includes Stromboli and Vulcano.about Hiera … Vulcanian Islands ‘Hiera’ is the ancient Greek name for Vulcano, one of the Aeolian Islands (themselves sometimes called the ‘Vulcanian Islands’).note mount Hecklebirg Spelled ‘Heckelberg’ in Germanic sources – another name for Mount Hecla, in Iceland, which in the seventeenth century was part of the Dano-Norwegian realm.note Styx In classical mythology, the waters of the Styx, one of the rivers (though sometimes described as a lake) of the underworld, were held to be deadly to humans and animals because of their icy coldness.about Phlegethon In Greek mythology, the river of fire in the underworld.about Pluto’s Court The Roman god of the dead and king of the underworld (the counterpart of the Greek Hades).note that poetical Infernus … tree In the fourth canto of the Inferno, Dante places the soul of Homer in the first circle of hell (limbo), where it is found in a wood wielding a sword.about Hermione The port town of Ermioni, in the southeastern part of Argolis on the Aegean coast.about Limbus patrum ‘Limbo of the Fathers’, one of the four parts of hell according to medieval theology (besides the ‘limbo of infants’, purgatory, and hell of the damned), and the place where those who had died in fellowship with God (and so the Patriarchs of the Old Testament) awaited the coming of Christ for their redemption and entry to heaven.about Ignatius’ parlour The ‘secret’ room in hell reserved for impious and heretical innovators in John Donne’s Ignatius His Conclave (1611).about Antipodes Vergilius (the Latin form of the Irish ‘Fergal’) of Salzburg (c. 700–784) was denounced to the pope by St Boniface (c. 675–754) for several of his beliefs, including that on the other side of the earth there was another race of men. ‘Antipodes’ here refers to this race, rather than to its location, and ‘Mentz’ here is Mainz.note Jerusalem where Christ died the middle of it Medieval maps typically placed Jerusalem at the centre of the world.about Delos An island in the Cyclades archipelago (although Delos here should actually be Delphi, regarded by the ancient Greeks as the centre of the world).note 200 Italian miles An ‘Italian mile’ varied in length, ranging between seven-eighths and one and a quarter English miles. According to the traveller and geographer Fynes Moryson, writing in 1617, an Italian mile was 1,000 paces in length (and so identical to a Roman mile), and an English one was 1,500 paces (1,760 yards).note in Diameter The Flemish theologian Leonhard Leys (Lessius, 1554–1623) calculated that the length of the cavern of hell could be as small as one, presumably Dutch, league, or four Italian miles.source Abraham’s bosom Heaven (after Luke 16:23).note voyage In Lucian’s Menippus, or The Descent into Hades, Menippus travels to the underworld and consults the blind prophet Tiresias about the good life.gloss accidents Occurrences, incidents.about Pontus In note ‘b’, the Senecan reference is to the ancient region on the south coast of the Black Sea, which had been the heartland of a Persian satrapy, and then a kingdom, before it became a Roman province.note complexions The balance of qualities in the whole body or in a particular bodily part, also referred to as the ‘temperament’ or ‘complexion’. An imbalance of these qualities was sometimes called a ‘distemperature’ (see the editor’s Introduction).about Perioeci People dwelling on opposing parts of the same meridian.about Quareca In note ‘c’, Quareca (or ‘Cuareca’) was a mountain range on the Isthmus of Panama, apparently named after its local chieftain, also called ‘Torecha’.about Zeilan Ceylon, now Sri Lanka.about Manamotapa The kingdom of Mutapa, located in what is now Zimbabwe and Mozambique. St.about Thomas’ Isle São Tomé in the Gulf of Guinea.gloss under the line At the equator.about Ister The lower course of the Danube.about Bithynia In antiquity, a region, kingdom and Roman province in northwestern Asia Minor.note Quivira, or Nova Albion in America Quivira was the name for a large region in North America including the area now covered by Oklahoma, Kansas and parts of Colorado, Texas and New Mexico. The precise location of Nova Albion (‘New Albion’) – somewhere on the Pacific coast of North America, and so named by Sir Francis Drake in 1579 during his circumnavigation – is disputed, but it may have been what is now San Francisco Bay.about Norumbega A mythical city, most commonly thought to be situated in what is now Penobscot Bay in Maine, New England.about Golden Fleece In 1616 Burton’s acquaintance William Vaughan, a Welsh scholar and poet who used the pseudonym ‘Orpheus Junior’, attempted to establish a colony in Newfoundland called Cambriol. In The Golden Fleece (1626), in which Burton makes an appearance as ‘Democritus Junior’, Vaughan presented the ‘Cambrioll Colchos’ (the latter term referring to the destination of the Argonauts) as the remedy for all human ills.about Topic stars Stars whose influence is exerted in a particular place.about Dodecatemories Each of the twelve divisions of the zodiac.note the Moon’s mansions In astrology, the twenty-seven or twenty-eight divisions (or ‘houses’) of the ecliptic, occupied by the moon on successive days.about Spruce In note ‘c’, Prussia.about Spahan Isfahan in modern-day Iran. 31 gr.: 31°, or ‘grades’.gloss inhabitable An obsolete word actually meaning ‘uninhabitable’.note the Brise Or ‘Breeze’, a north or northeast trade wind in the tropics.gloss evil-inhabited Sparsely populated.note refractionem Aristotelian climatology divided the earth’s atmosphere into three regions: the lower region, heated by the sun’s rays refracted from the earth, was warm and moist; the middle region, where water condensed into clouds, was cold and moist; and the higher region, being closer to heavenly fire, was hot and dry.about Sierra de Cadarama The Sierra de Guadarrama, a mountain range in central Spain running through the provinces of Ávila, Madrid and Segovia.about Lanes Plains (a corrupted form of the Spanish ‘Llanos’, or ‘Lanos’ in Burton’s source).about Potosa The Río de La Plata (River Plate), in Argentina and Uruguay, and Potosí in Bolivia – on which, see above, .about follow The ancient Greek astronomer Hipparchus of Nicaea (fl. 162–128 BCE), as reported in the works of Ptolemy, observed that the equinoxes occur earlier in each sidereal year, because of a slow, continuous change of the earth’s axis of rotation. As a result of this phenomenon, known as the ‘precession of the equinoxes’ or ‘axial precession’, the constellations of ‘fixed stars’ are gradually changing position in relation to the signs of the zodiac. The ‘first [point] of Aries’ referred to here, which is used to calculate longitudes in celestial navigation, and which moves westwards by one degree every seventy-three years, had moved into the sign of Pisces in antiquity. Burton’s main point here is that if the earth is the immobile centre of the universe, as in the geocentric model, then over time ‘diverse alterations’ will gradually occur to the regions of the earth as the constellations that influence them change their position.about The Philosophers of Coimbra The Jesuits of the University of Coimbra in Portugal, who at the instigation of Pedro de Fonseca (1528–99) and initially under the supervision of Emmanuel de Goes (1542–97), produced a series of commentaries on Aristotelian philosophy (the Conimbricenses) between 1592 and 1606.about Empyrean The higher region of the heavens.about Eccentricity In Renaissance astronomy, the ‘eccentricity’ of a planet is the numerical measurement of the elongation of its elliptical orbit (a circular orbit would have an eccentricity of zero).note those Medicean, Bourbonian, Austrian planets lately detected The ‘Medicean stars’ were the four moons of Jupiter, discovered by Galileo in 1610 and named after his future patrons; the ‘Bourbonian stars’ were sunspots mistaken for planets, named in honour of the French royal dynasty by the astronomer Jean Tarde in 1620; the ‘Austrian stars’ were also sunspots, named in honour of the house of Habsburg by the Belgian Jesuit astronomer Charles Malapert in 1633.about Sackbut A musical instrument with a slide like that of a trombone.about Coele-Syria Κοίλη Συρία, the ancient Greek name for Syria, or a region of it that included all of the country except Phoenicia.gloss manured Cultivated, managed.note dog days In ancient astrology, the ‘Dog Star’ (Sirius) was thought to induce disease, and it was also traditionally thought to cause madness in dogs. The ‘dog days’ were the hottest part of the summer, when the Dog Star was rising.gloss Lemmer Lemmings.about Princes of the air The name given to ‘aerial devils’ in 1.2.1.2 above.gloss exploded Rejects or condemns.source Sal, Sulphur, Mercury According to Paracelsus, the three elements of salt, sulphur and mercury (the tria prima) were the fundamental principles governing the qualities of objects and living things.about Salmoneus In classical mythology, the king of Elis (a region in the northwestern Peloponnese) who imitated the thunder and lightning of Zeus (Jupiter) by attaching bronze cauldrons and dried animal hides to the back of his chariot, and throwing lighted torches into the air while riding it. Zeus punished him with a real thunderbolt.gloss angust Compressed.about Manucodiatae In note ‘a’, birds of paradise – see above, .about Diaphanum A transparent body or transparency (hence the adjective ‘diaphanous’), sometimes used to describe the lower region of the heavens – on which, see below, .gloss cast Vomit violently.note parallaxes Apparent changes in the positions of the stars when viewed from different points on the earth.gloss orbs Orbits.note ♂ … ☉ The astrological symbols for Mars and the sun.note those fictitious first watery movers … Firmament A reference to the clear, ‘crystalline’ sphere in Ptolemaic astronomy – see above, – sometimes held to lie between the eighth sphere of the ‘firmament’, which contained the fixed stars, and the highest ‘empyrean’ sphere of heaven.about Eccentre Epicycles deferentes In Ptolemaic astronomy, planets moving in small circles (‘epicycles’) with their centres on the circumference of greater circles (known as ‘deferents’) could seem to be moving backwards around the earth.note circles equant Or ‘equalizing circles’, postulated by ancient astronomers to render planetary movements consistent with the hypothesis that celestial motion was uniform in velocity.about Homocentrics Spheres or circles concentric with others, or with the earth.about Colures The two principal meridians or ‘great circles’ of the celestial sphere, which intersect at the celestial poles: the equinoctial colure, which passes through the two equinoxes (the first points of Aries and Libra); and the solstitial colure, which passes through the two solstices (the first points of Cancer and Capricorn).about perform This anecdote, which ends with a fatal crash-landing and widespread ridicule for the Turkish Icarus, is not recorded by the Flemish diplomat and author Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq (1522–92), but originates in the Byzantine chronicles of Niketas Choniates (c. 1155–1217), who identifies the individual as a purported descendant of the biblical Hagar. Burton may have read about it in the General History of the Turks (1603) by Richard Knolles.gloss lets Hindrances, impediments.about Galileo’s glass A telescope, as used by Galileo.about many like Actually, not comets, but novae (newly discovered stars), which had been observed by Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) and Johannes Kepler (1571–1630). The new star discovered in 1604 by Kepler was actually in ‘Serpentarius’, the constellation now usually called ‘Ophiuchus’.about Axle-trees Or axes, the imaginary or geometrical lines forming the axis of revolution of a planet or celestial body.about Antarticum In note ‘e’, references to the Crux constellation in the Milky Way; and to the ‘Magellanic Clouds’, two large nebulae in the South Pole of the sky.note 29,000 Myriads 290 million (a ‘myriad’ being ten thousand).note like those 12,000 Isles of the Maldives There are actually around 1,200 islands in the Maldive chain of atolls, but the figure of 12,000 was reported in contemporary sources.note a substance or an accident Accompaniment – or more technically in Aristotelian language, a non-essential property or quality, and often contrasted with an essential ‘substance’.see Hermes See above, and .note in materiam primam In ancient Greek philosophy, prima materia is the ‘first’, fundamental matter from which all other matter is derived.gloss Neoterics Modern authors.gloss paradox A barely believable or strange doctrine.note videtur The calculations reported here are evidently faulty, or at least based on two incompatible sets of calculations. The Jesuit mathematician Christophorus Clavius (1537/8–1612) claimed that the circumference of the firmament was 1,017,562,500 miles in length, and that therefore – dividing 1,017,562,500 by 24, since the firmament completed its circular course every twenty-four hours – every star within it travelled 42,398,437.5 miles in one hour. Clavius also claimed, secondarily, that a point on the equator of the firmament travelled 176,660 miles in one unit of time, which he took to be fifteen seconds (the length of time it takes to say an Ave Maria, and equal to a 240th – not a 246th, which may be an error by Burton’s typesetter – of an hour); in one hour, therefore, a fixed point in the firmament would traverse 42,398,400 miles in an hour. Following this calculation gives the same figure as the distance covered by a man who rode for forty miles per day for 2,904 years – but in 203 years, travelling at the same speed, he would cover 2,963,800 miles, which is obviously far greater than the 706,640 (or 706,640.625, using Clavius’ initial calculation) miles covered by a point of the firmament in one minute. (None of these calculations take leap years into account.)note the whole world Here, the whole universe or cosmos. above ♀ and ☿, beneath ♄, ♃, ♂: ‘Above Venus and Mercury, beneath Saturn, Jupiter and Mars’.gloss absolves Completes.gloss solve all appearances Explain the observed facts.about those Alphonsine … tables This list begins peculiarly with two Greek heroes with constellations named after them, before introducing the astronomer Claudius Ptolemaeus (Ptolemy) – included, perhaps, because of his occasional (erroneous) association with the Egyptian dynasty of the Ptolemies – and Alfonso X, ‘the Wise’ (1221–84), king of Castile, León and Galicia, who sponsored the creation of the ‘Alfonsine Tables’ of astronomical data, which were influential across Europe until the seventeenth century.about Retrogradations Similar to parallaxes, but occurring when stars apparently move in a reverse direction from that which is normal.about Kepler, the Emperor’s Mathematician Kepler became imperial mathematician to the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II (1552–1612) in 1601; on the meaning of ‘mathematician’ here, see above, .about thence The ‘green children of Woolpit’, who, according to the chronicler William of Newburgh (1135/6–c. 1198), mysteriously appeared in this Suffolk village in the reign of King Stephen (1135–54), speaking an unknown language and eating only raw broad beans. olymp. 84.note anno tertio at Capuae Fluenta That is, in the third year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad, or 442/1 BCE (Pliny the Elder actually dates this to the second year of the seventy-eighth Olympiad, or 467/6). The claim that this occurred at ‘Capuae Fluenta’ (‘the streams at Capua’) is probably a slip, as the ancient sources identify the location of the meteorite in Greece as Aegospotami (‘Goat streams’), which in Latin would be ‘fluenta Caprae’.note Ancile or buckler in Numa’s time The small oval shield (ancile) fabled to have fallen from heaven in the reign of Numa Pompilius, the second legendary king of Rome, upon which the prosperity of the city was said to depend. In case the original was lost, Numa ordered eleven exact replicas to be made.gloss collects Infers, deduces.gloss stick not Do not hesitate.gloss in respect In comparison.note in his perspectives, Lunar Geography Informal references, which were both present in the first edition of the Anatomy (1621), to Kepler’s Dioptrice (1611) and his Somnium seu opus posthumum de astronomia lunaris, which was published posthumously in 1634 but had been mentioned in the Dissertatio cum nuncio sidereo (1610).note oppugn See above, . two Planets, ☉ and ☾: That is, the sun and the moon.about Daedalian Like Daedalus (‘Cunning worker’), who in Greek mythology was a supremely ingenious (mortal) inventor and craftsman.note the five upper Planets In the system of the German astronomer Nicolaus Reimers (Raimarus, 1551–1600), these are Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.about Planets without Orbs Planets unfixed to the spheres surrounding the earth that, in the Ptolemaic theory, carried the planets and stars with them in their revolution.about Jansonius Caesius hath illustrated in a sphere The Dutch cartographer Willem Janszoon Blaeu (1571–1638) made models of celestial globes in order to compare Ptolemaic with Copernican cosmography.note sound Drums and Trumpets The militaristic command is an authorial aside, commenting on the intellectual battles under discussion.gloss hoise Launch or lift.about Apelles The Jesuit astronomer Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650) used the pseudonym ‘Apelles’, referring to the celebrated ancient Greek painter Apelles of Cos, in a series of letters written in 1611 to report his observations of sunspots.note the Cyanean Isles in the Euxine Sea The Symplegades (‘Clashing Rocks’) in the Bosporus strait, which in Greek mythology were said to move around randomly, being unattached to the sea bed, and were successfully navigated by Jason and the Argonauts. The ‘Euxine’ is the Greek name for the Black Sea.note cum Apelle The author of De maculis in sole animadversis, et tanquam ab Apelle … Batavi dissertatiuncula (1612), calling himself ‘Batavus’ (‘the Dutchman’), is now thought to be Christoph Scheiner.note like the Philosophers in Lucian … abroad In Lucian’s Icaromenippus, or The Sky-Man, Menippus, dissatisfied with philosophers’ confused and contradictory speculations about the cosmos and the gods, makes himself wings and flies up to heaven to discover true knowledge. On his way up, he is accosted by the Moon, who asks him to relay her complaints about the absurd speculations of humans about her nature to Zeus, and threatens to remove herself from their view unless Zeus destroys the philosophers. Menippus delivers the message, and the god decrees that he will send his thunderbolt in the spring.gloss Theologasters Pseudo-theologians.note as he saith The Dutch poet and scholar Daniel Heinsius, in his Hercules tuam fidem (1617).source these gigantical Cyclopes will transcend spheres … doth In the Metamorphoses (1.151–62), Ovid refers to a story in which the giants of classical mythology attempted to seize the throne of heaven by piling mountains up to the stars: see below, . But there may be a simultaneous allusion here to Lucretius (5.110–25), where the giants are compared with those who, like Epicurus, give a rational account of the cosmos that is opposed to traditional religious belief.about Africk In Lucian’s Icaromenippus, or The Sky-Man (25–6), Zeus receives various prayers and sacrifices from human beings before issuing orders about the wind and weather. The image of Zeus painting the wings of butterflies, a touch of Burton’s own in the second edition (1624), alludes to the classical goddesses of the seasons (Horae), who were the ministers – or sometimes the daughters – of Zeus, and were often artistically depicted with butterfly wings.note the Turks’ Alcoran The Qur’an.about Mahomet … for him What Burton calls ‘a Pegasus’ is properly identified by his likely source here, Antoine Geuffroy’s Aulae Turcicae Othomannicique imperii descriptio (1577), as the ‘Alborac’. This is the Buraq, the winged horse of Islamic tradition said to have transported the prophet Muhammad into the heavens and back.about They have fetched Trajanus’ soul out of hell Note ‘b’ refers to the legend, recorded in the Speculum historiale by Vincent of Beauvais (d. c. 1264), that Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604) successfully petitioned God to liberate Trajan’s soul from hell, after being moved by a relief on Trajan’s column depicting the Roman emperor’s dispensation of justice to a widow. It became a frequently discussed example of the posthumous salvation of virtuous pagans.source bind and loose in heaven Retain and absolve sins – in contemporary Christian theology, interpreting Matthew 16:19, the power of judgement that belonged to the Church on earth and that would also be upheld in heaven.gloss quartermaster Someone who shares a quarter of responsibility with another or others.note Caecilius The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix presents a dialogue between the pagan Caecilius Natalis and the Christian Octavius Januarius.source Zacharias the Christian Allusions to the Contra Julianum by Cyril of Alexandria (c. 375–444 CE), a refutation of Julian the Apostate’s polemic against Christianity; the Recognitions, written in the fourth century CE and falsely attributed to Pope Clement I (d. 99), which reimagines the confrontation between Simon Magus and the apostle Peter described in Acts 8:9–24; and the Dialogus Ammonius of the lawyer and historian Zacharias Rhetor (465/6–c. 553), which stages a debate between the persona of the Christian author and that of his contemporary, the Greek Neoplatonist Ammonius.note hoo Similar to ‘how’, or ‘ho’ – an exclamation to attract attention, here also expressing astonishment or bewilderment.source novum Ecclesiastes 1:9 in the translation of the Latin Vulgate (where it is verse 10).note my game is sprung Made by the hunting hound to fly up into the air, where it is to be seized by the hawk.gloss election Free choice.see 1.2.2.5gloss conceited Ingenious, clever.note the Orcades The Orkney Islands.note temperature The balance of qualities in the whole body or in a particular bodily part, also referred to as the ‘temperament’ or ‘complexion’. An imbalance of these qualities was sometimes called a ‘distemperature’ (see the editor’s Introduction).gloss clownish A rustic, or peasant.gloss moors Marshes.about Fens This list of English locales with contrasting terrains includes the Lincolnshire Wolds, a range of hills in the county of Lincolnshire, and the marshy region of the Fens in East Anglia. On Romney Marsh, see above, .note hordes Probably the Nenets (or Samoyeds), an indigenous nomadic people in the Arctic region of Russia (‘hordes’ here means ‘nomadic tribes’.)about Sardis The capital of the ancient kingdom of Lydia and one of the principal cities of the Persian Empire (now Sart in Turkey).about Susa The capital of the region of Elam in what is now western Iran, and now the city of Shush; it was used by Cyrus the Great (reigned 559–530 BCE) as one of his capitals after he defeated the Babylonians in 539.about Persepolis The ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire in the reign of Darius I (522–486 BCE), located northeast of Shiraz in modern-day Iran.about Pasargada Pasargadae, built as the Persian capital in the reign of Cyrus the Great, also near Shiraz in modern Iran.about Ecbatana The ancient capital of the Medes, whose territory became part of the Persian Empire under Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE. It was located in what is now Hamedan in Iran.about Adrianople Or Hadrianopolis, now Edirne in the European part of Turkey, and the capital of the Ottoman Empire before the conquest of Constantinople in 1453.about Village Three scholarly abodes: the coastal villa of Pliny the Younger by Laurentum, near Ostia; the villa of Cicero at Tusculum, where he composed several of his philosophical works; and the lodgings at the Vatican palace of Paolo Giovio, where he wrote his Historiarum sui temporis libri XLV (1550–52).about past In Francis Godwin’s Catalogue of the Bishops of England (1601), cited in note ‘a’, the bishop of Exeter, John Veysey (c. 1464–1554), is criticized for stripping his see of most of its landed assets – although he was actually complying with requests issued by the royal court during the Reformation for leases and grants of episcopal properties. He was also the founder and benefactor of the grammar school attended by Burton in Sutton Coldfield (see the editor’s Introduction).about halitus William Camden refers in his Britannia (1586) to Ewelme Manor, in the Oxfordshire village of Ewelme. The house had been built by William de la Pole, duke of Suffolk (1396–1450), but had become a minor Tudor palace after being confiscated by Henry VII.note smokes In his Descriptio totius Italiae (1567), the Bolognese historian Leandro Alberti claims that the air of Venice is salubrious because of the fire and smoke being continually produced by the furnaces in its glassworks. On ‘Moorish’ here, see above, ; ‘qualify’ means ‘mitigate’, or ‘render less unpleasant’.gloss offends Harmed, hurt.about Lindley … Drakesly upon Trent These places, clustered in an area straddling the borders of Warwickshire, Leicestershire and Derbyshire, had a range of familial and personal connections for Burton. The village of Lindley in Leicestershire was his birthplace, and the nearby villages of Orton-on-the-Hill, Fenny Drayton, Caldecote (‘Caucut’), Amington, Polesworth, Weddington, Swarkeston (‘Swarston) and Drakelow (‘Drakesly’) were home to various members of Burton’s family and his acquaintances.gloss plat A patch or plot of land.note a Cotswold country Land like the Cotswolds, a range of hills mainly in Gloucestershire famous for their sheep-pastures.gloss fielden Open, level land, suitable for fields.note Champian Or, ‘here free and open, there constrained’. A ‘champian’ (or ‘champaign’) was an open and level plain, whereas ‘enclosed’ land had been converted from common ownership into private property.about place The coal owner Sir Francis Willoughby (1546/7–96) chose the position of Wollaton Hall and probably had a hand in its exuberant design, but the main architect was Robert Smythson (1535–1614).gloss Farmack Foremark.about Mount Edgemond Mount Edgecumbe.source in an excellent prospect Burton’s source here is the Constantini Caesaris selectarum praeceptionum de agricultura libri viginti (1538), the Latin translation of the Geoponika, a collection of Byzantine works on agriculture attributed by its unknown editor to the scholarly emperor Constantine VII (905–59 CE), although the main author in the original Greek compilation was Cassianus Bassus Scholasticus of the sixth century CE.about Cuddesdon in Oxfordshire … matched Cuddesdon Palace, built in 1634 by the bishop of Oxford, John Bancroft (mentioned in note ‘f’ as Burton’s former tutor), was destroyed in 1644 during the siege of Oxford in the Civil War, but it was later rebuilt.gloss coast Regions, places or countries.gloss Rustics Writers on rural matters.gloss Westchester Chester.about Vicenza Like other aristocratic dwellings in Costozza in the province of Vicenza, the house – described by the travel writer Fynes Moryson in his Itinerary (1617) – was connected to an extensive system of natural and artificial underground caves, the ‘Covoli di Costozza’.gloss pills Peels.about Benzoin, Ladanum, Styrax All fragrant resins used in perfumery and formerly in medicine, taken from the Styrax benzoin tree, the cistus plant and the Styrax officinalis tree respectively.gloss prefers Recommended.gloss sallow leaves Willow leaves.gloss fashions Manners and customs.note stock A tree-stump, as the type of something lifeless or lacking sensation – and so, figuratively, a blockhead or senseless person.gloss speculation Viewing or observation.about Liternum In the place cited here, Seneca praises the simplicity of the villa of Scipio Africanus the Elder – see above, – in Liternum, a Roman settlement in a swampy and malaria-infested region of Campania, and now the village of Lago Patria, near Naples. Elsewhere (Epistles 51), he contrasts it with the luxurious villas built at the resort of Baiae by other statesmen, such as Pompey and Julius Caesar.about the last king of Macedonia Perseus of Macedon (212–165/2 BCE) was defeated by the Romans at the Battle of Pydna in 168; he died in captivity, after gracing the triumphal procession of the Roman consul and general Lucius Aemilius Paullus in 167.about his son Scipio … Sulpicius Gallus The historical figures referred to here are Scipio Aemilianus (Scipio the Younger) – on whom, see above, and ; the brother and emissary of Eumenes II Soter, king of Pergamum (197–158 BCE); and the Roman politician, general and author of works on astronomy, Gaius Sulpicius Gallus (consul in 166 BCE).gloss passengers Travellers.source Hermon and Rameh in Palestina Mount Hermon, on the border between Syria and Lebanon; and possibly the town called ‘Rameh’, originally a village situated on a hill on the edge of what is now the Beit HaKerem valley in northern Israel (and probably the ‘Ramah’ mentioned in Joshua 19:29).about Collalto in Italy Mount Collalto, in the South Tyrolean region of northern Italy.about the top of Taygetus The highest mountain in the Taygetus range, in the Peloponnesian peninsula of southern Greece.about Acrocorinthus, that old decayed castle The Acrocorinth (‘Upper Corinth’) was the acropolis overlooking the ancient city of Corinth. It had been occupied continuously since at least the eighth century BCE, and had various Byzantine as well as medieval Frankish fortifications – which are probably the ruins referred to here.about Radway Grange Glastonbury Tor, a hill near Glastonbury in Somerset; Belvoir (‘Fine View’) Castle in Leicestershire; and Radway in Warwickshire, which is at the foot of Edge Hill.about Walesby in Lincolnshire … Countess Dowager of Exeter In 1624 Burton was granted the benefice of Walesby in Lincolnshire by Frances Cecil, the Dowager Countess of Exeter (1580–1633), but as note ‘d’ records, he resigned it in 1631 (see the editor’s Introduction).note other In his Icon animorum (1614), the poet John Barclay describes the view from Greenwich Hill in London. The word ‘tower’ here may refer to the Palace of Placentia, which was known as ‘Duke Humphrey’s Tower’ (after Humphrey, duke of Gloucester, 1390–1447) and would later make way for the Royal Observatory, although the use of the word ‘tower’ as a synonym for ‘tor’ (hill) is not uncommon in this period.gloss promiscuous Mixed and disorderly.gloss success Result, upshot.gloss Trencher Plates or platters, often round, on which meat was served.note maculae and faculae In astronomy, ‘maculae’ are dark spots on the surface of the sun, whereas ‘faculae’ are light spots.
